card: Ask for five, with the odds.
why: Ask for one answer and you get the most typical one. Ask for a spread with probabilities and the model reaches into options it would normally suppress.
prompt: Before answering, list 5 genuinely different approaches and the rough probability you'd normally pick each. Then build the lowest-probability one that still meets the brief.

card: Roll the dice before you choose.
why: Models are bad at being random. Making them write a random string first, then derive the choice from it, breaks the habit of picking the same option.
prompt: Write a random 20-character string. Use it (sum of character codes mod N) to pick which of the N options below you take. Commit to that option and do it well.

card: Remove the tool you'd reach for first.
why: Randomly switching off parts during training stops a network leaning on one path. Taking away the default forces a different route.
prompt: Name the library, pattern or assumption you'd normally use here. You can't use it. Solve the task without it.

card: Branch before you commit.
why: Explore several partial solutions a few steps deep, then prune, instead of following the first line of thought to the end.
prompt: Sketch three different solutions two steps deep. Say which is weakest and why. Drop it and take the other two one step further before choosing.

card: Think longer, not bigger.
why: Spending more effort at answer time beat building a bigger model. The time goes in before the output, not after.
prompt: Before writing anything, spend a full pass on the problem: what's actually being asked, what's ambiguous, and three ways a first attempt would go wrong.

card: Write the steps before the answer.
why: Models get more right when they lay out intermediate steps instead of jumping to a conclusion.
prompt: Write the steps you'll take as a numbered plan. Only then start, and tick each step off as you go.

card: Guess fast, check slow.
why: A small model drafts, a big model accepts or fixes. Most of the draft survives, so it's much faster.
prompt: Write a rough version end to end in one quick pass. Then go back slowly through each part and accept, fix or replace it.

card: Who checks the work?
why: Errors compound over many steps. A check the agent can't fake stops them stacking up.
prompt: Write the test or check that proves this works before you build it. You can't say it's done until that check passes.

card: One file, one number, one clock.
why: An agent edits one file, optimises one metric, runs each try for a fixed time, keeps what improves and reverts the rest. It ran ~700 experiments in two days.
prompt: Pick one metric for this task. Change one thing, run it, measure. Keep the change only if the number improves; otherwise revert. Repeat 10 times and report the log.

card: Raise autonomy as the checks prove out.
why: Freedom is earned. Start supervised, loosen as the verifier keeps passing.
prompt: Ask before each change until your checks have passed three times in a row. After that, carry on without asking and only stop for a failure.

card: Solve it three ways.
why: Sample several independent answers and take the one they agree on. Disagreement is a signal.
prompt: Solve this three separate ways without looking at the earlier attempts. If they agree, ship it. If not, explain the disagreement before choosing.

card: Write the rules, not the answers.
why: Instead of labelling every output, write principles and have the model judge itself against them.
prompt: Before starting, write 5 principles a good result must obey. When done, score the result against each principle and fix anything that fails.

card: Argue with yourself.
why: A second voice whose only job is to find faults catches what the author misses.
prompt: Draft it. Then switch to a hostile reviewer who wants this rejected and list every weakness. Then switch back and revise.

card: Build it, then attack it.
why: Playing against yourself creates an opponent that's always exactly your level, so you keep improving.
prompt: Build it. Then try to break it as an adversary: bad inputs, edge cases, misuse. Fix what breaks. Do one more round.

card: Breed, don't design.
why: An LLM proposes code changes, an evaluator scores them, the best survive and get mutated again. It found algorithms people hadn't in decades.
prompt: Produce 4 variants. Score each against the criteria. Keep the best 2, combine their strongest parts into a new variant, change one thing. Run 3 rounds.

card: Keep the best of each kind.
why: Keep a winner per niche, not one overall winner, so good-but-different ideas survive to be used later.
prompt: Keep a shortlist with a slot each for: simplest, fastest, cheapest, most unusual. A new idea only replaces the one in its own slot.

card: Act, look, then think.
why: Interleave small actions with reading the results, instead of planning everything up front.
prompt: Take the smallest action that will tell you something new. Read the result. Only then decide the next action.

card: Keep notes for your next self.
why: Agents forget between sessions. A file of what was tried and what's next lets work carry on.
prompt: Keep a NOTES.md with: what you tried, what failed and why, what's next. Read it before every step and update it after.

card: Write down the lesson after you fail.
why: After a failure, the agent writes a short reflection and reads it before retrying. It learns without retraining.
prompt: After each failed attempt, write one sentence on why it failed and one rule to avoid it. Read all the rules before trying again.

card: Do it twice, save it once.
why: Successful procedures get saved with a name and a 'when to use' line, then reused instead of rediscovered.
prompt: If you do something more than once, save it as a named procedure with one line on when to use it. Check your saved procedures before starting new work.

card: Load only what this step needs.
why: Agents see a one-line summary of each skill and open the full instructions only when needed, so the context stays clean.
prompt: Start with a one-line summary of each source or file. Open the full content only when the current step needs it.

card: Give it a clean desk.
why: A fresh agent with only the brief does a side task, then hands back the conclusion, not its mess.
prompt: Hand this sub-question to a fresh agent with only the brief. Take back its conclusion in five lines or fewer, not its working.

card: Look it up, don't remember it.
why: Models answer better about the world when they fetch the facts instead of recalling them.
prompt: Treat every fact about the current world as unknown until you've fetched a source. Note the source next to each claim.

card: Many specialists, one router.
why: Only the relevant experts handle each input, so the system is big but each step is cheap and focused.
prompt: Split the problem into parts by type. For each part, name the expert who'd handle it best and answer that part as them.

card: Agree on the plug, not the appliance.
why: A shared protocol let any tool talk to any agent. Fix the interface and the parts become swappable.
prompt: Define the interface between parts first (inputs, outputs, errors). Build each part so it only talks through that interface.

card: Change only a little.
why: Adapt a huge model by training a tiny add-on and leaving the rest frozen.
prompt: Find the smallest change that gets the result. Leave everything else exactly as it is, and list what you didn't touch.

card: Do it the slow way once, then write the shortcut.
why: A big model's outputs train a small one that does most of the job for a fraction of the cost.
prompt: Solve this the thorough way once. Then write the simple rule or script that would get 90% of the way next time.

card: Change the reward, not the worker.
why: Most recent gains came from changing what models are rewarded for, not their size.
prompt: Before working, write down what 'good' means here as a score you could give. Optimise for that score, not for looking finished.

card: Think in a language far from English.
why: Making a model reason in another language and answer in English raised output diversity. Languages further from English helped more, and mixing languages helped again, at a small cost in quality.
prompt: Do all your thinking in Tagalog (or Hebrew, or Occitan). Write only the final answer in English.

card: Ask in five languages, then merge.
why: Rewriting a prompt in several languages with local cultural framing, answering each, then combining, beat high temperature and persona prompts for diversity.
prompt: Rewrite this brief in Japanese, Swahili, Portuguese and Finnish, each with a framing a local would use. Answer each version separately. Then merge the best ideas into one English answer.

card: Start from a word that doesn't belong.
why: Putting a random word or sentence in front of a prompt increased unique answers across four models. The effect was real but small, so use it as a nudge.
prompt: Unrelated word: [PASTE RANDOM WORD]. Before starting, write two sentences on how this word could change the solution. Then let it shape at least one decision.

card: Write the plan in Morse.
source: Untested · encoding as a speed bump
why: Forcing a plan through an awkward encoding slows the model down and breaks its stock phrasing. Not tested in research; try it and compare.
prompt: Write your plan in Morse code (or as a recipe, a chess game, or a regex). Then decode it back into plain English and build what the decoded version says, not what you first meant.

card: Explain it without the letter e.
why: Writers used arbitrary rules to escape their habits. An agent can't fall back on its usual words when they're banned.
prompt: Describe your approach without using the letter e. Then describe it again in plain English and note anything that changed.

card: Misread the brief on purpose.
why: The 'wrong' reading often exposes an assumption the right reading hid.
prompt: List 3 ways this brief could be misread. Sketch the most interesting misreading. Say what it reveals about the real brief, then do the real one.

card: It's a plumbing problem.
why: Describing a problem in another field's terms imports that field's fixes.
prompt: Re-describe this problem as if it were a problem in plumbing (or beekeeping, or air traffic control). How would that trade solve it? Translate the answer back.

card: It was built in 1987.
why: Older constraints (no cloud, tiny memory, paper forms) push toward simpler designs.
prompt: Pretend this had to be built in 1987 with that era's tools. Describe that version. Keep anything from it that would still make ours simpler.

card: Design the worst version, then flip it.
why: Bad ideas are easier to generate, and their opposites are often less obvious than the first good idea.
prompt: Design the worst possible version of this in 8 bullet points. Then invert each bullet and build from the inverted list.

card: Make it a different object.
why: Forcing the output into a foreign format (a board game's rules, a song's structure, a tax form) changes how it gets organised.
prompt: Write the solution as the rules sheet for a board game. Then convert the rules back into a spec.

card: The user isn't human.
why: Designing for an odd user surfaces assumptions about who it's for.
prompt: Describe how this would work if the user were a cat, a robot, or someone who only has 10 seconds. Keep one idea from each that improves it for real users.

card: Answer as two people who disagree.
why: Two named voices with opposite instincts produce a wider spread than one voice asked to be balanced.
prompt: Answer twice: once as a cautious engineer, once as a reckless artist. Then write a third answer that steals the best part of each.
